variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: A chat system accepts a message once, stores it durably, orders it within one conversation, and makes it available to every intended recipient device. A live WebSocket makes delivery feel immediate, but the durable conversation log is what lets the system recover after a disconnect, retry, or server failure.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “What is a chat system?”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Commit before accepted
pairs.detail: Authorize, deduplicate, assign the conversation sequence, and commit the message plus its outbox event before telling the sender it was accepted.
pairs.explanation: Authorize, deduplicate, assign the conversation sequence, and commit the message plus its outbox event before telling the sender it was accepted.

pairs.label: Order one conversation
pairs.detail: Give each conversation one logical sequencing owner.
pairs.explanation: Give each conversation one logical sequencing owner. Global ordering across unrelated conversations is unnecessary and expensive.

pairs.label: Replay after failure
pairs.detail: Clients reconnect with a durable cursor, fetch missing sequence ranges, and apply messages idempotently before resuming the live stream.
pairs.explanation: Clients reconnect with a durable cursor, fetch missing sequence ranges, and apply messages idempotently before resuming the live stream.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Use the full lesson’s worked examples and interactive labs to explore the trade-offs behind these questions.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Commit before accepted: Authorize, deduplicate, assign the conversation sequence, and commit the message plus its outbox event before telling the sender it was accepted. Order one conversation: Give each conversation one logical sequencing owner. Replay after failure: Clients reconnect with a durable cursor, fetch missing sequence ranges, and apply messages idempotently before resuming the live stream.

variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: A chat system accepts a message once, stores it durably, orders it within one conversation, and makes it available to every intended recipient device. A live WebSocket makes delivery feel immediate, but the durable conversation log is what lets the system recover after a disconnect, retry, or server failure.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “What does the data model protect?”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Conversation log
pairs.detail: Store immutable message events by (conversation_id, bucket, sequence).
pairs.explanation: Store immutable message events by (conversation_id, bucket, sequence). A time or sequence bucket prevents one long-lived conversation from creating an unbounded physical partition.

pairs.label: Membership
pairs.detail: Store member role, join sequence, leave sequence, and membership version.
pairs.explanation: Store member role, join sequence, leave sequence, and membership version. A fanout event carries the version used when the send was authorized.

pairs.label: Device cursor
pairs.detail: Track the highest contiguous delivered sequence per (conversation, user, device) so reconnect fetches a range instead of scanning all history.
pairs.explanation: Track the highest contiguous delivered sequence per (conversation, user, device) so reconnect fetches a range instead of scanning all history.

pairs.label: Presence lease
pairs.detail: Map a user-device to gateway and lease expiry.
pairs.explanation: Map a user-device to gateway and lease expiry. Rebuild it from live connections; never use it as proof that delivery succeeded.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Use the full lesson’s worked examples and interactive labs to explore the trade-offs behind these questions.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Conversation log: Store immutable message events by (conversation_id, bucket, sequence). Membership: Store member role, join sequence, leave sequence, and membership version. Device cursor: Track the highest contiguous delivered sequence per (conversation, user, device) so reconnect fetches a range instead of scanning all history. Presence lease: Map a user-device to gateway and lease expiry.

variants.prompt: From the lesson section “What are delivery semantics?”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Accepted
pairs.detail: The ordered message and outbox event are committed.
pairs.explanation: The ordered message and outbox event are committed. The sender may stop retrying this client message ID.

pairs.label: Delivered
pairs.detail: At least one intended device confirms a contiguous sequence at or beyond this message.
pairs.explanation: At least one intended device confirms a contiguous sequence at or beyond this message.

pairs.label: Read
pairs.detail: A client reports the highest sequence the user viewed.
pairs.explanation: A client reports the highest sequence the user viewed. The server advances, never decreases, the watermark.

pairs.label: Synced
pairs.detail: Every active device eventually fetches missing ranges; long-retired devices expire under policy.
pairs.explanation: Every active device eventually fetches missing ranges; long-retired devices expire under policy.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Use the full lesson’s worked examples and interactive labs to explore the trade-offs behind these questions.

Synced: Every active device eventually fetches missing ranges; long-retired devices expire under policy.

variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: A chat system accepts a message once, stores it durably, orders it within one conversation, and makes it available to every intended recipient device. A live WebSocket makes delivery feel immediate, but the durable conversation log is what lets the system recover after a disconnect, retry, or server failure.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “What makes the system reliable?”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Gateway failure
pairs.detail: Clients reconnect with jitter to a healthy gateway and replay after their durable cursors.
pairs.explanation: Clients reconnect with jitter to a healthy gateway and replay after their durable cursors. The failed process owns sockets, not messages.

pairs.label: Conversation-owner failure
pairs.detail: Pause or queue sends until a new owner holds a higher fencing token.
pairs.explanation: Pause or queue sends until a new owner holds a higher fencing token. Never let two regions assign the same sequence range.

pairs.label: Fanout backlog
pairs.detail: Keep accepted messages durable, prioritize live text over optional signals, batch by gateway, and expose delivery delay instead of dropping work silently.
pairs.explanation: Keep accepted messages durable, prioritize live text over optional signals, batch by gateway, and expose delivery delay instead of dropping work silently.

pairs.label: Presence or push outage
pairs.explanation: Continue accepting and storing messages. Rebuild presence from sockets and let clients recover history without depending on push.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Use the full lesson’s worked examples and interactive labs to explore the trade-offs behind these questions.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Gateway failure: Clients reconnect with jitter to a healthy gateway and replay after their durable cursors. Conversation-owner failure: Pause or queue sends until a new owner holds a higher fencing token. Fanout backlog: Keep accepted messages durable, prioritize live text over optional signals, batch by gateway, and expose delivery delay instead of dropping work silently. Presence or push outage: Continue accepting and storing messages.

variants.title: Give each part its job

A live WebSocket makes delivery feel immediate, but the durable conversation log is what lets the system recover after a disconnect, retry, or server failure.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “What trade-offs define this design?”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Commit before ack vs early ack
pairs.detail: Commit-before-ack adds storage latency but makes accepted meaningful.
pairs.explanation: Commit-before-ack adds storage latency but makes accepted meaningful. Early acknowledgement is faster only by shifting message-loss risk to the user.

pairs.label: Home region vs multi-writer
pairs.detail: A conversation home simplifies total order and deduplication.
pairs.explanation: A conversation home simplifies total order and deduplication. Multi-writer regions reduce local write latency but require conflict semantics users can understand.

pairs.label: Push fanout vs pull on sync
pairs.detail: Push gives low online latency; pull makes offline recovery simple.
pairs.explanation: Push gives low online latency; pull makes offline recovery simple. The hybrid design pushes to live gateways and always retains cursor-based history.

pairs.label: Receipt rows vs watermarks
pairs.detail: Per-message receipt rows answer detailed audits but explode writes.
pairs.explanation: Per-message receipt rows answer detailed audits but explode writes. Monotonic per-device watermarks compress the common "read through sequence N" case.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Use the full lesson’s worked examples and interactive labs to explore the trade-offs behind these questions.

Home region vs multi-writer: A conversation home simplifies total order and deduplication. Push fanout vs pull on sync: Push gives low online latency; pull makes offline recovery simple. Receipt rows vs watermarks: Per-message receipt rows answer detailed audits but explode writes.

variants.prompt: With 1 billion logical messages per day and a 5x peak multiplier, approximately what peak ingress should the command path handle?
options: 11,600 messages/s
58,000 messages/s
232,000 messages/s
5,000,000 messages/s

variants.prompt: Why does the design route one conversation to one fenced sequencing owner at a time?
options: To make presence strongly consistent across every region
To give unrelated conversations one global total order
To avoid storing message IDs on client devices
To prevent competing owners from assigning conflicting order within that conversation
variants.explanation: Conversation-local ownership provides the order users need without globally coordinating unrelated chats. Fencing prevents a stale owner from continuing to write after failover.
